segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods bowed to the goddess in all beings, and she answered Shumbha with a vow.

One syllable: hum. That's all it takes in the sixth chapter. Furious at her vow, Shumbha sends a general named Dhumralochana with an army and an order: drag her here by the hair. The general shouts at her to come quietly. She answers, in paraphrase: you're strong, and you've brought an army. If you take me by force, what can I do? He rushes at her. She makes one sound, hum, and he's burned to ash. Her lion takes care of the army. And the goddess is about to show a face the story hasn't shown yet.
screen: `DRAG HER HERE BY THE HAIR.` → `ONE SOUND: HUM.` → `A FACE NOT SEEN YET.`

segments.voice: In the seventh chapter Shumbha sends Chanda and Munda, the servants who first told him of her, with a bigger army. They find her seated on her lion on a golden peak, smiling, and come at her with bows and swords. Her face goes dark with anger, dark as ink. And from her frowning forehead another goddess springs out. The text describes her plainly. Kali. Dark, gaping mouth, lolling tongue. Thin, wrapped in a tiger skin, a garland of human heads, a skull-topped staff and a sword in her hands. Her roar fills the sky. She tears into the army, swallowing elephants whole with their riders and bells, crunching chariots in her teeth. She seizes Chanda by the hair and cuts off his head, then Munda's, and carries both back to the goddess, laughing, as a gift. The goddess names her: because you've brought me Chanda and Munda, you'll be known as Chamunda. So Kali comes not from outside but from the goddess's own brow, at the moment the threat comes close. The same goddess who smiled on the mountain carries this fierce face inside her. And that closes the first week of year four. A king and a merchant who couldn't let go. Vishnu's sleep. Every god's gift, and a lion. A shape-shifter pinned. Kindness to enemies. The goddess in all beings. And now Kali. One goddess, seen from more and more sides.
screen: `HER FACE GOES DARK AS INK.` · `KALI SPRINGS FROM HER BROW.` · `CHANDA AND MUNDA: CHAMUNDA.` · `THE WEEK: ONE GODDESS, MANY SIDES.` · then, large: `THE FIERCE FACE WAS INSIDE HER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone or something you'd stand up for, picture it threatened for just a moment, and notice what rises, a straighter back, a firm jaw, without acting on it: strength, not cruelty. Then let calm come back alongside it, breath by breath, the way the goddess was smiling and fierce at once. If you pray, bow to the goddess or to God in your own words; if not, let the breath hold both.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its sixth and seventh chapters: one syllable that burns a general to ash, and Kali, springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda.
Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Seven days in, and the goddess keeps showing new faces. Week one of year four, done.

notes: Last day of week one of year four; looks back over 1062–1067. Covers chapters 6 and 7.

Chapter 6 paraphrased: Dhumralochana sent with an army to drag the goddess by the hair; her reply (if you take me by force, what can I do to you?); reduced to ashes by the sound hum (huṃkāra); the lion destroys the army. The army's size is given in the text and deliberately not spoken. 'Smoke-Eye' renders the name; confirm.

Chapter 7 paraphrased: Chanda and Munda find her smiling on her lion on a golden peak of the Himalaya; her face becomes dark as ink; Kali emerges from her forehead with sword and noose, skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), garland of heads, tiger skin, emaciated, gaping mouth, lolling tongue, red eyes; she devours elephants with riders and bells, crushes chariots; kills Chanda and Munda; offers the heads; the goddess names her Chamunda. Confirm.
Kali's appearance is described plainly, as the text does. Confirm the tone suits the path and that a Keeper from a Shakta lineage would recognize her.
